title: Hassler v. Circle C Resources
summary: The Wyoming Supreme Court abandoned judicial rewriting of unreasonable noncompetes and directed judgment for the employee because this covenant’s duration and geographical reach were unreasonable.
notes:
The precedent overruled was Hopper v. All Pet Animal Clinic, Inc. (Wyo. 1993), which had adopted the liberal blue-pencil rule; the decision is Hassler v. Circle C Resources, 2022 WY 28, issued 25 February 2022, and under it a noncompete with an unreasonable duration or territory is void in its entirety as against public policy.

The covenant's territorial term as written barred competition for 24 months in any geographic area in which Circle C marketed or had marketed its services during the year before separation, which is why the district court thought narrowing was needed before it could enforce.

sections.Parties: Circle C provided habilitation services to disabled clients. It sued its former employee, Charlene Hassler, for continuing to provide residential care to a client after leaving its employment.
sections.Material Facts:
Hassler was hired in 2015 to care for a nonverbal adult client in her own home. Circle C trained her for about a month. Her agreement restricted competing work and service to Circle C clients for twenty-four months across seven named Wyoming counties and potentially other areas. It also asked courts to substitute the maximum reasonable restrictions if the written restrictions were unenforceable.

The client’s mother became dissatisfied with Circle C’s day services and changed providers. The client continued living in Hassler’s home while residential services were billed through another provider and Hassler obtained her own Medicaid provider number. After Circle C threatened enforcement, Hassler stopped paid services for a period, although the client remained in her home and family members provided much of the care. Circle C eventually sued for its projected lost profit. It actively operated in only two of the listed counties and did not defend the full twenty-four-month term as necessary on appeal.
sections.Procedural History: On competing summary-judgment motions, the district court reduced the restriction from seven counties to two and from twenty-four months to twelve, then awarded Circle C $94,742.10. The Wyoming Supreme Court reversed and remanded for judgment for Hassler, overruling its earlier adoption of the liberal blue-pencil approach.
sections.Issue: Should a court rewrite an unreasonable employment noncompete to make it enforceable, including when the parties expressly request that rewriting?
sections.Holding: No under the Wyoming rule adopted in this 2022 decision. The unreasonable duration and territory made this noncompete invalid, and the court would not rescue it by drafting a narrower covenant.
sections.Reasoning:
The court balanced freedom to contract, freedom to work, and the public interest in competition. An employer could seek protection from unfair competition through reasonable restrictions tied to legitimate interests, but was not entitled to protection from ordinary competition. It bore the burden of establishing the restrictions’ reasonableness.

The earlier liberal blue-pencil rule had allowed courts to narrow excessive terms. The court concluded that this encouraged employers to overreach: employees and prospective employers might obey intimidating restrictions even when a court would eventually reduce them. Judicial rewriting also created uncertainty about the actual obligation and used courts to improve a drafter’s bargain. A clause requesting rewriting could not obligate judges to perform that role.

Because the duration and territory were undisputedly unreasonable, the court did not need to decide whether Circle C otherwise had a legitimate protectable interest. The holding concerns the noncompete and the historical Wyoming doctrine. It is not a nationwide declaration about all restrictive covenants, and the book’s later note about a proposed federal rule is not the separate 2026 supplemental reading.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Hassler links the substantive limits on a restraint to the remedy for excessive drafting. The choice between rewriting and nonenforcement changes the incentives created by the rule.

topics.public-policy: Freedom to work and competition limit enforcement of the private restriction.
topics.noncompetes: The employer must justify duration, territory, and the interest protected.
topics.severability: The court rejects liberal rewriting of this covenant rather than substituting its own narrower agreement.
topics.governing-law: The state high court expressly changes its own precedent; the decision must be identified by jurisdiction and date.
topics.precedent: The court expressly overruled its own 1993 decision in Hopper, making the case a clean example of a state supreme court abandoning precedent on policy grounds.
